pz1991.note: For 1991 Yamaha went back to round jet sizes and printed the part number for each. At 8,000-10,000 ft in the warmest column it also sets the pilot (idle mixture) screw to 2.0 turns. The chart groups the bands into three drive line settings: 0-2,000 ft, 2,000-6,000 ft and above 6,000 ft, which match the clutch tables.

piped.intro: A pipe moves the power peak up, so the clutch has to shift higher to keep the engine on it. Nothing here is a Yamaha figure: it is what riders report on their own piped sleds. No DG-specific clutch setup was found; the most detailed write-up is a 1990 Phazer II with a PSI pipe.

rows.piped: Red-green (about 1.75 kg/mm, 35 kg or more preload, three engagement shims), red-silver or red-brown. A blue-white reached only about 7,000 rpm.
82M (Exciter) weights, which shift higher. The 8V0 (1984-89) and 87F (1990) weights are the weakest.
45 degree helix from a 570 Exciter or an 80s VMax
One tooth up on the top sprocket, to 18

piped.cautions: Springs and weights are tuned per clutch: settings for the YPZ primary do not carry over to a YXR, and the stock primary was revised around 1991-93 (pinned weights, then riveted). Check which you have before ordering. Change one thing at a time and tach the shift rpm on a long, wide-open pull.

magneto.install: Clean any oil or grease off the crankshaft taper with a cloth dampened in thinner before fitting the rotor. Fit the Woodruff key and stator plate, pass the magneto leads through the crankcase hole and seat the grommet, and line up the timing mark on the stator plate with the crankcase seam (1991 supplement p.16).
magneto.partsSource: Stator and rotor part numbers are each model's Generator fiche at Rich's Yamaha (same OEM catalogue and model slugs as Partzilla), read 2026-11-24. Every stator, coil and rotor except 88F-85550-00-00 was listed as discontinued that day.
magneto.partsNote: Phazer and Phazer II use the same stator, 88F-85510-00-00, from 1986 to 1993, and 8BL-85510-00-00 for 1994-95; the coils inside it (source 86M-85511-00-00, lighting 8H8-85513-20-00 and 82M-85514-20-00, pulser 82M-85580-20-00) do not change. The rotor is 8V0-85550-21-00 through 1990, then 88F-85550-00-00 on recoil-start sleds and 88H-85550-00-00 on electric-start and ST sleds (the 1991 ST is listed with 88F). The Venture XL has its own 88T stator and rotor (8BK stator 1994-95). The Venture GT is listed with the Phazer II LE stator, coils and 88H rotor, except that the 1993 GT shows the 88T stator.

torque.note: Pairs were read from the Clymer tables and checked on 2026-11-19 against Yamaha's own PZ480 table (factory manual p.8-8), which gives every value in N-m, m-kg and ft-lb. Yamaha works in m-kg: its N-m figure is the m-kg value times 10, and its ft-lb figure is m-kg times 7.2. That is why the larger values look about 2% off an exact N-m conversion (60 N-m converts to 44.3 ft-lb, but Yamaha prints 43). The printed figures are correct as Yamaha specifies them; the m-kg column is shown where the factory table gives it.

springs.source: Yamaha Technical Bulletin S88-007, 9 Sept 1988 — 'All Models: Primary and Secondary Clutch Spring Information'
springs.conflict: Partzilla lists 90501-45534-00 as the primary spring for the 1986-1989 Phazer. Two independent factory documents disagree with it: bulletin S88-007 and Table 3 of the high-altitude chapter both give the PZ480 primary as 90501-52798, and both put it at 25.8 kg set weight in red-blue. The evidence now runs 2-to-1 against the Partzilla number, which is most likely a supersession. Still measure free length and wire diameter before ordering. The 1991 supplement adds a clue: 90501-45534 is the standard primary for the 1991 Phazer II ST (blue-green, 25.0 kg preload, 1.06 kg/mm, 85.1 mm free length), close in preload to the 25.8 kg PZ480 spring but much softer in rate, so it is not a like-for-like part.
springs.secondaryConflict: The two sources disagree on the standard secondary spring colour: bulletin S88-007 lists 90508-50654-00 for the PZ480 as yellow-blue, while Table 3 of the high-altitude chapter calls the PZ480 secondary white. The bulletin gives a part number and full dimensions, so it is the more specific source, but check the twist angle — Table 3 specifies 60 degrees (B-1) — rather than going by colour.

primary.usedOn: EC540 — the number Partzilla lists for the 1991 Venture XL

springs.secondaryNote: Rates marked * are in kg·mm/rad (torsional), not kg/mm — the bulletin says torsional force matters more for a secondary than compression force, so those two columns are not directly comparable.

altitude.source: Chapter Four, High-Altitude and Rear Suspension Adjustment (PZ480), pages 114-134
altitude.powerLoss: About 3% of power per 1,000 ft of elevation gain. The manual's worked example: an engine making 40 hp at sea level makes roughly 38.8 hp at 1,000 ft and about 29.5 hp at 10,000 ft.
altitude.factoryBaseline: The PZ480 carburettors are jetted at the factory for sea level at 32 to -4 °F (0 to -20 °C). Everything else is a correction away from that. This is the 1984-89 calibration: Yamaha's own 1984-89 chart puts the stock #143.8 at sea level from about -13 °F to 59 °F (-25 to 15 °C). From 1990 the factory charts are richer, and the stock #143.8 becomes the 300-2,000 ft jet in cold weather.
altitude.clutchThreshold: Above 6,000 ft (1,800 m) the clutch needs re-specifying. Left alone, it bogs at the point of belt engagement and bogs again in deep snow — both of which kill drive belts.

clutch.verdict: For the Phazer the entire high-altitude clutch change is one part: the primary spring. Weights, engagement and shift rpm, and the secondary all stay standard.

gearing.verdict: The PZ480 gearing does not change for altitude. The chapter text says a gear change may be needed above 6,000 ft, but Table 6 lists the Phazer's high-altitude gearing as identical to standard — only the EX570 actually changes. Re-gear for terrain and snow, not for elevation.

gearRatios.note: Upper figure is the ratio, lower is the chain links required. Ratios are driven ÷ drive and are exact. X marks a combination the chart gives no chain length for.
gearRatios.caution: Chain-link counts come off a low-resolution scan. The standard 17/29 with a 64-link chain is independently confirmed by Table 6 and by the Partzilla chaincase listing; treat the others as a starting point and measure.
gearRatios.guidance: Smooth snow with few rough sections suits a smaller (numerically lower) ratio. Poorer snow or rugged terrain suits a higher one.

suspension.principle: Ski pressure — the load on the skis relative to the load on the track — is the primary factor controlling handling. Too little and the front floats, steering goes vague and the sled wanders under steady throttle. Too much and it plows in corners and the skis knife in on the straight. Hard surfaces want more ski pressure so the skis bite; soft tacky snow wants less so they do not sink.
suspension.levers: Ski pressure goes up by softening the front springs or pulling the front end down with the stopper band; it goes down by stiffening the front springs or extending the band.

adjustments.effect: Hole 1 is longest, hole 5 shortest. A longer setting gives less ski pressure and more speed but poorer manoeuvrability and straight running. A shorter setting gives more ski pressure and steering stability, at the cost of starting acceleration.
Hole 1 allows maximum suspension travel. Shortening the strap reduces ski pressure for higher speeds and cuts suspension travel for more traction, but costs steering stability.
1 is soft — works well over small bumps and gives more positive steering. 3 is hard — reduces bottoming over large bumps but reduces steering. Rotate the cams at the end of the spring.
1 is softer, giving better traction over small bumps at the cost of positive steering. 3 is for large bumps, at the cost of traction.

Sets weight transfer to the track. Upper suits most trail riding. Lower is for deep snow, and is the drag-racing setting where traction matters more than steering — at full throttle on the lower hole the skis will lift off the ground.
Varies how fast spring rate rises. Hole 3 gives the fastest rise and the firmest ride; hole 1 the slowest.

carbTuning.source: Chapter Four, Carburetor Adjustment (PZ480 and 1987 EX570), pages 118-124

circuits.controls: Pilot jet and pilot air screw
Mid-range — main nozzle and needle jet

carbTuning.airScrewWarning: It is a pilot AIR screw, not a fuel screw, so the directions are the opposite of what people usually assume: clockwise LEANS the mixture, counter-clockwise RICHENS it. Warm weather or higher altitude — turn it clockwise. Very cold — counter-clockwise.
carbTuning.jetNumbers: For both pilot and main, a larger number is a richer mixture.
carbTuning.idleProcedure: Seat both pilot air screws lightly, back them out 1-1/2 turns, warm the engine, set the throttle stop to 2,000-2,500 rpm, then turn the air screws counter-clockwise until peak rpm is reached and reset the throttle stop to the 1,600 rpm idle spec. If off-idle pickup is poor, or performance is off at altitude or in extreme cold, fit larger pilot jets.
carbTuning.torsNote: Whenever idle speed is changed, redo the Throttle Over Ride System (T.O.R.S.) adjustment.
carbTuning.airboxWarning: Do not run the engine without the air silencer or air box fitted — the manual warns this can cause engine seizure. Worth weighing against the common advice to gut the airbox for a carburettor swap.
carbTuning.mainJetAccess: Mains can be changed without pulling the float bowl: remove the drain plug and washer at the bottom of the bowl and the main jet is behind it. The engine will be hot and fuel will spill, so have an extinguisher and a helper.

plugReading.look: Light tan or grey deposit, no gap wear or erosion
plugReading.means: Carburetion, ignition and heat range all correct

plugReading.look: Soft, dry, sooty black deposit over the firing end
plugReading.means: Too rich, plug heat range too cold, over-retarded timing, ignition failure, or low compression

plugReading.look: Black insulator tip, damp oily film, carbon layer over the nose, electrodes not worn
plugReading.means: Too much oil in the fuel (jetting or oil pump adjustment), wrong oil type, ignition failure, heat range too cold, or still breaking in

plugReading.look: Badly worn electrodes, premature gap wear, grey or white blistered insulator
plugReading.means: Heat range too hot, or: lean mixture (main jet or oil pump), timing too advanced, cooling fault, air leak, overtightened plug, or missing plug gasket
Wrong oil type, excess carbon in the chamber, or a clogged exhaust port and pipe
Almost certainly preignition — check for carburettor mounting or intake manifold leaks and over-advanced timing; a too-hot heat range is also possible
Needs more voltage to fire under hard acceleration — replace

carbTuning.finalWord: The manual is explicit that these are guidelines only, that they vary with altitude, temperature and snow conditions, and that the condition of the spark plugs is the determining factor when changing jets.

identify.trackLenNote: The 1991 Phazer II ST is a long-track sled: Yamaha gives 1,054 mm (41.5 in) on the ground against 865 mm (34.1 in) for the standard Phazer II (1991 supplement, General specifications), although the parts data in this app lists the 121 in track part number for it.
identify.where: Frame number: stamped on the right-hand side of the frame (tunnel), just below the front of the seat. Engine number: right-hand side of the crankcase. The first three characters identify the model; the rest is the production number.
identify.source: Yamaha 1990 PZ480P/EP manual p.1-1; 1991 PZ480R/ER/STR supplement p.1; 1993 PZ480T/ET/STT supplement p.1; 1996 supplement p.1; Clymer 1984-89 Chapter One.
identify.gaps: The manuals checked give no starting numbers for 1986-89, 1992, 1994-95 or any Venture. For those, use the features below and the Year changes tab.
identify.note: Starting serial numbers are the first unit of that model. A frame number matches only when the sled still has its original frame; an engine may have been swapped from another year.

interchange.note: Same part number means a direct swap by Yamaha's own catalogue. A different number does not prove it will not fit, only that Yamaha listed something else; check the dimensions before buying.

facts.title: Drive belt changed for 1992
facts.text: Every 1986-91 Phazer, Phazer II and the 1991 Venture list belt 89X-17641-01-00; every 1992-95 model lists 89L-17641-01-00. Aftermarket listings agree on the split: the 1986-91 belt is about 43.3 in outside circumference by 1.25 in wide (Clymer gives 1,099 mm / 43.3 in, 31.6 mm new), the 1992-on belt about 44.2 in by 1.38 in. They do not cross over.

sources.label: Parts data in this app (model belt part numbers)

facts.title: Aftermarket belts
facts.text: 1986-91: Dayco HPX5000 (43.313 x 1.25 in), listed for Phazer 1984-89, Phazer II 1990-91, Phazer II ST 1991 and Venture XL 1991. 1992-95: Ultimax MAX1118M3 (44 3/16 x 1 3/8 in), listed for Phazer II, LE, ST and Venture GT/XL 1992-93 and Venture XL 1994-98; Gates G-Force 43G4340, which replaces 89L-17641-00-00 and lists Phazer II and Venture 1992-96. Retailer fitment lists, not Yamaha's; check the year against your sled.

facts.title: Spark plug
facts.text: NGK BR9ES, gapped 0.7-0.8 mm (0.028-0.031 in). That is the 1984-89 manual figure; the 1990-95 engines carry the same engine part numbers. The R means resistor type; keep it.

facts.title: Front end and struts
facts.text: The first-generation TSS front end is shared across the SRV, VMax 540, Exciter, Ovation and Phazer II with different spring rates; 1984-89 Phazers do not share struts and springs with the VMax and SRV. Detail on the Mods & upgrades tab.

troubleshooting.source: Clymer 1984-89 Yamaha snowmobile manual, Chapter Two (Troubleshooting): Operating requirements, Ignition system, Fuel system (Figure 45), Engine, Two-stroke pressure testing, Power train, Skis and steering, Track assembly, Table 1. Checks are listed in Clymer's order. Written for the 1984-89 PZ480; the 1990-95 sleds use the same engine and drive family, so the checks carry over, but use the figures for your model.

checks: Check the obvious first: engine stop switch in RUN, tether switch fitted (1984), not flooded from too much choke, fuel in the tank, plug wires on.
If it has sat a while: clean or replace the plugs, check the battery (electric start), then work along the fuel supply from the tank. Drain stale fuel and try a fresh tank.
Spark test: plug in its cap, base grounded on the head, crank it. You want a fat blue spark. Hold the lead with insulated pliers.
No or weak spark: check connections at the coil and battery, then test the main, engine stop and tether switches, and the throttle override switches (1985-on).
Then test the ignition coil, pickup coil and source coil against the resistance table below.
items.note: The ignition is the weakest of fuel, compression and spark. Clymer: more problems come from ignition than anything else, so check it before touching the carburettors.

checks: Air vent in gas cap closed

items.note: A choke stuck closed floods it; one stuck open makes it hard to start.

items.symptom: Cuts out or will not run after throttle, cable or idle work (1985-on)
checks: Throttle Over Ride System (T.O.R.S.): a switch at the carburettor and one at the throttle lever are wired into the ignition (Clymer Figure 15). If they disagree, the engine is cut. Check throttle cable free play (1.0-2.0 mm) and that the throttle snaps shut at full lock.
Redo the T.O.R.S. adjustment whenever idle speed is changed (Yamaha), then test the switches as Clymer describes in Chapter Eight before replacing the CDI.
items.note: Riser and cable changes are the usual way to upset it.

checks: Inlet control arm (float arm) set incorrectly
Obstructed carburettor pulse or vent lines
Loose carburettor mounting or a faulty flange gasket
Only under heavy load (accelerating): usually a defective plug
Dirty carburettor, dirty or worn inlet seat and needle

items.symptom: Flat spot: dies for a moment when the throttle opens, then recovers
checks: Low-speed mixture too lean or too rich
Air leaks in the fuel line or fuel pump
Choke or throttle valve not working fully
Ignition timing at full advance, checked running (Chapter Three). Right on the dial gauge but wrong running points to an ignition part
Galling piston, wrong piston clearance, worn or sticky rings
Loose bolts or leaking gaskets at head, cylinder or crankcase; crankcase and crank seals (pressure test)
items.note: A noticeable drop in speed can be the first sign of a seizure.

checks: Mixture too rich or too lean
Loose, worn or leaking inlet seat and needle, or a bad seat gasket

items.symptom: Hard starting and poor running, but compression is good
checks: Crankcase leak. A two-stroke needs the crankcase sealed, and a compression test does not show it.

Pressure test: block the intakes and exhaust ports, pump to about 9 psi through a plug hole. A good engine loses no more than 1.5-2 psi over several minutes; losing 1 psi in a minute means a serious leak. The labyrinth seal links both cylinders, so test them together.
Find leaks with soapy water: crankshaft seals, plugs, head joint, base joint, carburettor base, crankcase joint.
Loose engine, suspension or steering mounting bolts
Worn motor mounts (forum-reported; see Known problems on the Mods tab)
Fan belt: check tension and damage every 20 hours (Yamaha's table). This is the cooling system on a fan-cooled engine.
Spark plug of the wrong heat range (stock NGK BR9ES)
items.note: Overheating and lack of lubrication cause most engine mechanical failures.

checks: Lean mixture at or near full throttle
Plug of the wrong heat range, or overheated plugs
Carbon deposits on piston and head (decarbonize once a season)
Excessive oil in fuel, poor fuel, lean mixture (preignition)
items.note: Under the hood at high rpm you will not hear it. Clymer says this inaudible detonation is usually behind engine damage with no apparent cause.
Read the plugs: the Clutch, gearing & suspension tab has a plug-reading table.

items.symptom: Seizure, or a rattle from the top end
checks: Treat a top-end rattle as an early sign of seizure.
Scuffing above the rings usually means too much heat; below the rings usually means lack of oil.
Causes: wrong piston clearance or ring gap, compression leak, wrong oil, wrong plug heat range, wrong timing, oil pump not set or not bled, any overheating.
Bleed the oil pump after the tank runs dry, a hose is disconnected, or the sled is laid on its side.

items.symptom: Belt not running smoothly in the primary
checks: Drive sheave face rough, grooved, pitted or scored

items.symptom: Uneven belt wear, or edge cord failure
checks: Primary and secondary out of alignment (check sheave offset)
Slipping from a stuck or frozen track

items.symptom: Belt too tight at idle (sled creeps)

checks: Worn or damaged secondary sheave buttons
Sheared key on the brake disc

items.symptom: Chaincase noisy, chain slipping, or fast chain and sprocket wear

checks: Track touching rivets in the tunnel (wrong rivets fitted before)
Lugs too tall for the drivers (forum-reported; see Track fit)

items.symptom: Rear idlers turning on the shaft

electrical.title: Ignition and charging resistance (PZ480)
electrical.note: Test at room temperature, 68 F (20 C). Lighting output is measured with the engine at operating temperature. The 1984-89 column is Clymer Table 2-1, checked 2026-11-24 against Yamaha's PZ480 factory table (p.8-10). The 1990 column is Yamaha LIT-12618-PZ-50 pp.8-13 and 8-14; ranges are the printed nominal plus or minus its tolerance.
electrical.warning: The two factory manuals print different pickup, source and grip warmer coil resistances, although the parts catalogue lists the same stator (88F-85510-00-00) and source coil (86M-85511-00-00) for 1986 through 1993. The 1990 page also prints the pickup and source figures with no unit ("14" and "556"); ohms are assumed. Neither has been confirmed on a known-good stator, so treat a reading inside either column as plausible, and a reading far outside both, or an open or shorted coil, as the fault.
rows: Grip warmer lighting coil, yellow/black to black
11.8 V at 3,000 rpm; 15 V max at 8,000 rpm

maintenance.source: Yamaha LIT-12618-PZ-50 (1990 PZ480P/EP), Periodic maintenance table and Lubrication intervals, pp.2-1 to 2-3. The 1984-89 schedule in the Clymer manual (Chapter Three, Tables 1 and 2) uses the same 20/40/80-hour intervals and the same items.
maintenance.headNote: Retighten the cylinder head every 10 hours from first use (footnote to Yamaha's table). Clymer: retighten the head nuts after the 10-hour break-in.
maintenance.breakIn: After a rebuild: first 10 hours at no more than 3/4 throttle, vary the speed, avoid hard acceleration and wet snow, then check every engine and chassis fastener (Clymer, Chapter Three).
maintenance.ventureNote: The Venture's touring-chassis items (rear suspension, battery, lights) are not in this table; no VT480 manual has been checked.

items.item: Fuel and pulse hoses: loose connections, breaks
Oil delivery hoses: loose connections, breaks
Cylinder head and exhaust pipe decarbonization
Spark plug condition, gap and cleaning
Wear of drive track wheel sprockets
Bends in front and rear axles
Wear and breaks in wire covering
Battery fluid, specific gravity and breather pipe (electric start)

lube.lube: Gear oil API GL-3, SAE 75 or 80

lube.item: Brake wire end stopper and brake lever

clutchRange.source: Clymer 1984-89 Yamaha snowmobile manual, Quick Reference Data, Transmission specifications: V-belt automatic, ratio range 3.5:1 to 1:1 (PZ480).

calc.stGearing: Factory gearing differs on the long-track sled: the 1991 Phazer II ST (PZ480STR) left the factory on 17/33 (1.941), the standard and LE on 17/29 (1.706). Yamaha 1991 supplement, General specifications.
calc.autolube: Every PZ480 has Yamaha Autolube oil injection, and Yamaha calls for no premix (Clymer, General Information: Lubricant). Gasoline: 87 pump octane minimum (Clymer, Chapter Three).
calc.premixNote: Premix is for sleds with the oil injection removed or disconnected, or a safety mix on top of working injection. Riders who removed injection on piped sleds report 32:1 (forum-reported). Use one brand of two-stroke oil and mix in a clean can, not the sled's tank.

mods.note: Collected from rider forums (mostly TotallYamaha) and period press. Unless a line is tagged official or press, it is one or more riders reporting their own sled, not a Yamaha figure. Measure, read the plugs, and change one thing at a time.

items.title: Aftermarket single pipe
items.text: Aaen, DG and PSI pipes are the usual first mod. A pipe moves the power up: PSI pipes are reported to run best at 7,250-7,300 rpm, so the clutch must be raised to match (see Clutching). One rider ran 147.5 mains for years on Aaen-piped 1985-87 Phazers.

items.title: Reed valves
items.text: Boyesen reeds are widely reported as a worthwhile gain; FMF reeds are also used. A rider notes the stock reeds open around 5,000 rpm.

items.title: Porting and pistons
items.text: Piped and ported engines are reported at about 80 hp. One builder dyno claim: 63 hp at 6,750 rpm from piston work alone, 78 hp at 7,750 rpm with an aftermarket pipe. One experienced rider warns against cutting the heads.

items.title: Stock output
items.text: A 1989 magazine comparison lists the Phazer II at 55+ hp in its table and just under 60 hp in its text; riders commonly quote 53 hp. No Yamaha horsepower figure has been found.

items.title: Fix the lean midrange first: Yamaha's nozzles
items.text: Riders quote a Yamaha service bulletin from about 1996: primary nozzle 80L-14489-00-00 (two 0.9 mm holes instead of one 1.0 mm) and main nozzles 1A (leaner) or 2A (richest) against the standard 3A. Richest for steady mid to full throttle is the 80L primary with the 2A main. The hole in the standard primary must face the air box. Riders call the 80L 'the fix everyone has done' on piped sleds.

items.title: Jetting a piped sled
items.text: The usual starting point is two main sizes up from the stock jet for your altitude, pilots up from #95 to #100-105, and the 80L / 2A nozzles. Then read the plugs.

items.title: Burn-down warnings
items.text: One rider burned a piston within six miles on 148 mains with the 80L primary. Another traced melted pistons to belt dust blocking the carburettor vent tubes. Check plugs after every change and keep the vent tubes clear.

items.title: Flat slides (disputed)
items.text: Reported: Mikuni TM38 and TMX flat slides, racked VMax 600 flat slides, 38 mm Lectrons, and Aaen 42 mm then 38 mm kits. Twin flat slides need a two-cable throttle (an Exciter throttle block is one fix). One dyno claim puts the gain at about 2.7 hp, and only with a gutted airbox, which Yamaha's manual warns against. Some riders say flat slides woke the engine up; others say the nozzle fix is enough. Details on the Carb swap tab.

items.title: Cold air intake
items.text: The usual approach keeps the airbox. Take out the factory plate that blocks the louvered hood panel and the small reverse cone inside the box, then run a PVC tube with a scoop up to the louvers. One rider had to put foam in the tube as a filter, because otherwise it pulled in enough snow to freeze the carbs. Pulling the airbox off for pod filters on the stock carbs changes the mixture (one owner says it leans out, another found it running fat), and owners call the stock carbs' midrange hard to tune; engine-bay air also swings between cold and very hot. Nobody posted stock-carb jet changes for an intake mod, so read the plugs. A vent cut into the clutch cover was blamed for burning a hole in the PTO piston.

items.title: Two versions of the stock primary
items.text: Yamaha's 1990 manual (p.4-1) shows weights held on pins with bushings. The 1993 supplement (p.9) shows a revised primary: weights riveted in place, collars on the rollers, and a shim under the primary spring, with spring free length 76.8 mm (78.7 mm on the ST). The 1991 supplement already lists the newer W176A weight numbers (87F-W176A-00 against 1990's 87F-17632-00). Identify which style you have before ordering weights or springs.

sources.label: Yamaha 1990 manual p.4-1; 1991 supplement p.26; 1993 supplement pp.9-12

items.title: YPZ and YXR primaries
items.text: Riders and PSI's pipe instructions give separate settings for a YPZ and a YXR primary: silver/silver spring in the YPZ, and 4,300-4,500 engagement / 7,600 shift for PSI's YXR setup. Yamaha's 1984-89 manual calls the Phazer's clutch the Y-PZ. Which 1986-95 sleds, if any, left the factory with a YXR is not confirmed. Springs and weights are tuned per clutch, so a setup for one does not carry over to the other.

items.title: Roller secondary
items.text: Several builds swap the stock slider secondary for a roller secondary. A 1992-or-newer Exciter or Phazer secondary is named as a fit in one swap thread, which suggests the secondary also changed around 1992 (unconfirmed).

items.title: Raising the shift rpm for a pipe
items.text: From a detailed write-up for a 1990 Phazer II with a PSI pipe: aim for 7,250-7,300 rpm shift and at least 4,000-4,500 engagement. Red-green primary spring (about 1.75 kg/mm, 35 kg or more preload, three engagement shims), or red-silver. 82M (Exciter) weights shift higher than the 87F (1990 Phazer) or 8V0 (84-89), which are the weakest. A 45 degree helix from a 570 Exciter or an 80s VMax. One tooth up on the top sprocket, to 18. The owner then reached 7,000 rpm with a blue-white spring and 7,250-7,300 with a red-brown.

items.title: Other reported clutch setups
items.text: A 1991 with a red-pink spring and 82M-90 weights engaged at about 4,200 and pulled to about 7,300. A silver/silver primary in the YPZ clutch (PSI's recommendation with its pipe) was called fast. PSI's YXR clutch targets 4,300-4,500 engagement and 7,600 shift.

items.title: Gearing down
items.text: 17/33 is the common gear-down, called 'dang near unstoppable' in flat country; 16/35 has been suggested for deep snow. Going from 8- to 7-tooth drivers is about the same as dropping two teeth on the top gear. One long-tracked piped sled lost about 15 mph of top speed. The sprocket and chain part numbers are on the Clutch, gearing & suspension tab.

items.title: Factory track sizes
items.text: Camoplast's chart: Phazer 1984-89 15 x 116, Phazer II 1990-2001 15 x 121, Phazer II ST 1991-94 15 x 136, all 2.52 in pitch. Camoplast gives no lug height for these rows; Sledtrack's copy of the Camso data lists 1 in for the Phazer II and ST.

items.title: Lug height and drivers
items.text: Strong agreement across four threads: 1.25 in is the safe choice on the stock 8-tooth drivers. 1.5 in on 8-tooth is at the limit (one rider has about 3/8 in clearance on a 136 x 1.5); others say it slaps the tunnel and bulkhead. 7-tooth drivers allow 1.5-1.75 in, maybe 2 in, though one rider says they bend the track too tightly. Every Phazer before the 1999 Pro Action skid has 8-tooth drivers. The Track fit tab checks this for you.

items.title: Long-tracking a first-generation Phazer
items.text: Move the 116 skid back 2.5 in and use WPS rail extensions to reach 121 or 136. A Phazer II skid needs the rear mounts relocated and the upper crossover idlers added.

items.title: Skid swaps
items.text: Reported: Ski-Doo SC10 II and SC10 III in 1985 and 1989 Phazers (front holes moved back about 2 in; rear stays or moves forward 1/2 in), an Exciter Pro Action in an 1989 Phazer, a Ski-Doo SC4 136, and a 1997 VMax skid. One rider measured the Phazer II skid at 29 3/4 in centre to centre against the SC4's 23 7/16 in.

items.title: Tunnel extensions
items.text: No bolt-on extension for these chassis turned up for sale. Riders have one bent from sheet metal at a local shop (one quotes about $75-80; it needs a brake) or cut one from a donor tunnel, and lengthen the rear bumper with tubing. The factory extension from the 136 in Phazer II ST fits but rarely turns up used. Price the skid, rail extensions, track, drivers and gearing together: one rider who priced a 136 x 1.5 in conversion chose a 121 x 1.25 in instead because the extra 15 in "costs a lot more".

items.title: Long-tracking a Phazer II
items.text: A 133 in skid from a 1998 Polaris RMK X10 went into a 1990 Phazer II after narrowing it about 1/2 in, mounted further back to run a 136. Another rider estimated about $300 and a few hours to fit a 1999 Polaris Mountain Max skid with a 136 x 1.5 in track. Nobody reports a true bolt-in, and a Phazer II 121 skid needs work to go into a 1984-89 chassis. Hartman once listed a 116-to-121 kit for first-generation sleds (not confirmed current).

items.title: Track swap experiences
items.text: 1 in lugs on a 1993 Phazer II: lots of clearance at the drivers. 1.25 in on the stock 8-tooth drivers: fits, but refitting the drivers is "a workout". A 136 x 1.75 in Polaris track on a 1991 with 7-tooth drivers: fits but tight, and the owner found 7-tooth drivers almost too low geared once the sled was piped. For 1.5 in, riders recommend 7-tooth drivers with no chaincase change and expect some loss of top speed. Measure your own driver clearance before buying.

items.title: TSS front-end interchange
items.text: The first-generation TSS on the SRV, VMax 540, Exciter, Ovation and Phazer II uses the same spring length with different rates. One rider believes the Venture 480, VK540 II and Enticer II share it too (unverified). First-generation Phazers (84-89) do not share struts and springs with the VMax and SRV.

items.title: Front spring colours
items.text: Green for the 1990 Phazer II (two 1990 sleds checked had green-dot springs), red for 83-up VMax, gold for the 87 Exciter, yellow for the 90 Exciter, light blue for the 93 Ovation. Bender Racing once sold ten TSS rates from black (softest) to no-colour (hardest); out of production.

items.title: Struts, skis and stance
items.text: Fox gas struts and shocks are a common upgrade. Struts from the 1994-96 500, 600 and 700 raise the belly for deep snow. Plastic skis (Camoplast lightweights, or factory skis shimmed) and 6 in carbides are common. Ski stance is 36.2 in for 1990-95 and was widened to 38.6 in for 1996; CB Performance and others sold TSS widening kits. The Exciter bulkhead differs from the Phazer's.

items.title: Handlebar risers for standing
items.text: On a 1986 Phazer the stock cables allow about 2 in of rise; any higher and the brake applies when the bars are turned. Taller risers (3.5-5 in) need longer brake, throttle and oil-pump cables, and nobody posted Phazer part numbers for longer ones. A rider raising the bars on a 1992 Phazer II also went to new cables. Another suggests moving the steering post forward instead, which means giving up the airbox. After any change, check at full lock both ways that the brake releases fully and the throttle snaps closed.

sources.label: TotallYamaha thread 103673 (SX Viper, a different sled; same cable limit)

items.title: Running boards
items.text: Wider custom running boards come up in build lists, along with a shortened seat, removable rear rack, short windshield, handlebar hooks and LED bulbs, but nobody posted dimensions, materials or a finished install for these chassis. Treat it as your own fabrication project.

items.title: Motor mounts and belts
items.text: Worn motor mounts let the engine move, which misaligns the clutches and eats belts. One rider's mounts went at 10,000 km. Check them whenever belts keep failing, and check sheave distance and offset after replacing them.

items.title: Water in the bottom end
items.text: The 485 is widely called very reliable, but connecting rod and crank bearing failures happen, often after water or condensation pits the bearing surfaces. One family lost four engines from a 1993 Phazer II, the first after it went under water. Keep water out and fog the engine for storage.

items.title: Oil pump setting
items.text: One rider calls the stock oil pump 'pretty lean' and sets it to the rich side. Check the pump cable free play against the manual's 21-23 mm first.

items.title: Burned pistons on piped sleds
items.text: Lean midrange with a pipe is the reported cause. See Carburetion above.

items.title: Factory manuals
items.text: Yamaha LIT-12618-PZ-50 covers the 1990-96 Phazer II, with supplements for the 1991, 1993 and 1996 models; the 1984-89 PZ480 manual and Clymer's 1984-89 manual cover the first generation. The Venture manual is LIT-12618-01-41 with supplement LIT-12618-01-69. The figures in this app come from these; SOURCES.md lists which page each one is read from.

items.title: Parts and track fitment
items.text: OEM parts diagrams are linked from the Parts tab (Partzilla). Track sizes by year come from Camoplast's Yamaha chart.

items.title: Forums
items.text: TotallYamaha is where most of this tab comes from and has the deepest Phazer archive. Snowest, Hardcore Sledder, Snowmobile Forum and Vintage Sleds also have Phazer threads but block automated reading, so they are not covered here. Most search results for "Phazer" now concern the 2007+ four-stroke, which shares nothing with these sleds.
